findings.where: First screen, the one action: the 'Mark.Moseley@MMMinfra.com →' button (p16)
findings.fault: The page's one action goes nowhere. Its link points to '#', not to a mailto: address, so clicking the button that says 'Write to me' does nothing. Its arrow promises that something will happen.
findings.who_objects: The bank official who decides to get in touch. They click and nothing opens, so they have to copy the address by hand. Mark loses the one thing the page is for.

findings.where: First screen, the five topic pills under the lead (PPP Law, Infrastructure, Development banks, Governments, Risk allocation; p10–p14), at desktop and phone
findings.fault: These pills are static, but they look clickable. Each draws its own outlined capsule like a filter chip or a button, and they sit just above the real action. Clicking 'PPP Law' to see Mark's work on it does nothing. They also add a third layer of things that look actable between the message and the one action.
findings.who_objects: The official, who expects 'PPP Law' or 'Risk allocation' to lead to Mark's writing on that subject and gets a dead click. That makes the site feel half-built to someone judging how careful an advisor is.

findings.where: Article specimen: the caption under the TV-studio photo running into the subhead 'So, what are the key chapter topics?', and the three-item list running into the rule and the PDF link, worst at phone
findings.fault: The brief's own test of rhythm fails here. The caption sits right on top of the subhead with almost no space, so it reads as part of the heading. The list is set much tighter than the paragraphs, so its wrapped lines crowd together at phone width. It then runs straight into the rule and the lecture link. Image, caption, list and subhead each break the vertical rhythm.
findings.who_objects: The founder and Angélique. The brief asks that the type rhythm hold when an image, a caption, a list or a subhead is added, and this specimen shows it does not. The reader of a long PPP article also gets a cramped, uneven page.

findings.where: First screen, the blue field: the diagonal stripe pattern over the whole hero, at desktop and phone
findings.fault: The hero is covered in diagonal hatching. The page's own Texture tile says 'No texture: one flat field, no grain and no gradient', so the page contradicts its spec. The hatching looks like an engineering drawing or a hazard pattern, and it makes a quiet field busy behind the heading and lead.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for one blue field, nothing that looks 'in-your-face techy', and a ground that is not busy (Mark finds busy sites off-putting). The official sees a pattern that suggests engineering, not legal advice.

findings.where: First screen: the giant ghost 'PPP' letters behind the heading. At phone, a cut-off 'PP' bleeds off the right edge beside the heading
findings.fault: Huge pale letters sit right behind the main line and overlap it. The heading looks double-printed, and the reader's eye snags on the overlap. At phone width the cut-off letters look like a rendering fault. Neither the palette nor the texture tile mentions this element.
findings.who_objects: The official reading Mark's opening sentence, which is the one message on the screen. The overlap muddies it and looks like a gimmick, not the restraint of a senior legal advisor.

findings.where: Article specimen: the orange-red list bullets and the orange-red 'Streamlining the PPP Process…' link, against the blue 'Play again' link
findings.fault: An orange-red accent appears that the palette tile rules out ('Four colours and no accent'). The page now has two link colours, house blue in one place and orange-red in another, so link colour no longer means one thing.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for the house blue and grey as the only ink. The reader also has to learn two link colours on one site.

findings.where: First screen, phone (390 px): the order of photo, heading and action
findings.fault: At phone width the first screen is the logo, the nav, a large portrait and its caption. Mark's line starts at the very bottom of that screen, and the 'Write to me' action is about one and a half screens down. Neither the message nor the action is on the first phone screen.
findings.who_objects: The official who opens the link from LinkedIn on a phone. They see a face with no statement of what he does and no way to reach him until they scroll. The research asks for one message and one action on the first screen.

findings.where: First screen, the lead and the area around the action
findings.fault: There is no checkable proof near the action. The lead claims Mark advises development banks and governments, but the first screen names no body, place, year, talk or article. Nothing shows the claim is real before the visitor is asked to write.
findings.who_objects: A development bank official who hires against terms of reference. They look for named bodies, regions and dated work before they get in touch, and a claim without evidence reads as marketing.

findings.where: Header, desktop and phone: the logo's mark and lettering reversed to white on the blue field; also the Texture tile
findings.fault: The logo appears in all-white, a version the client is not known to hold. On this blue ground the logo's blue lettering would not show, so the logo has been recoloured rather than given a supplied version.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose logo is blue and grey. A white version needs his agreement before it is used, under the house's never-recolour rule.

findings.fault: There are two nav items whose difference the visitor can't tell. Both sound like Mark's writing, so the visitor has to guess which one holds what they want.
findings.who_objects: The official looking for Mark's work on PPP law. They don't know whether to open Articles or Blog and may check both, or neither.

findings.where: Article specimen title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law' (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The apostrophe in 'World's' is set as an upright tick with a gap after it, so it reads 'World' s' at display size.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader of a legal advisor's article title. Loose punctuation at the largest size on the page reads as carelessness.

findings.where: Type pair, desktop: 'Source Sans 3' in the right column
findings.fault: The 'Source Sans 3' sample sits lower than the Gelasio line beside it, aligned to neither its baseline nor its top. It looks like it slipped out of place.
findings.who_objects: The founder reviewing the style tile. The misalignment makes the specimen look unfinished.
